title: To school when old
hook: Seneca goes to lectures as an old man: learn as long as you don't know (Letters 76)
carry: learn as long as I live

segments.voice: Yesterday: let memory be sweet. Your line was sweet memory. Which happy story did you tell, and which friend did you spend a few greedy minutes with? Day four hundred seventy-one.

Picture a lecture hall full of twenty-year-olds, and in the third row, an old man with a notebook, taking it all down. Some of the students glance back and smirk. Seneca was that old man. He was one of the most famous writers in Rome, a former adviser to the emperor, rich beyond counting, and in the seventy-sixth letter he tells Lucilius that he's been going to school. Five days running, he's sat through the lectures of a philosopher named Metronax. And he knows exactly what people are saying about it. Today: to school when old.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE THIRD ROW.` → `THE STUDENTS SMIRK.` → `FIVE DAYS AT METRONAX'S SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: First, the mockery. Seneca reports it himself: look at him, an old man, going back to school. He doesn't deny it. He just doesn't care. Second, his rule. Learning, he says, should last as long as your ignorance lasts. In Latin: tamdiu discendum est, quamdiu nescias. And if we believe the proverb, he adds, that means as long as you live. There's never a day when you've finished not knowing something. Third, the theater next door. On his way to the lecture, Seneca passes the theater of Naples, packed to the rafters. People crowd in to hear a flute player, or to decide who's the better musician. The philosopher's school, meanwhile, has only a handful of listeners, and the crowd thinks those few have nothing better to do. Seneca finds this a little sad, and a little funny. Fourth, why it matters. Seneca isn't saying an old person needs to catch up. He's saying the posture of a student is the posture of a living mind. Seneca at sixty-something, with a notebook, is a quiet rebuttal to anyone who thinks they're too old, too busy or too established to begin something new.
screen: `LOOK AT HIM, AN OLD MAN IN SCHOOL.` · `LEARN AS LONG AS YOU DON'T KNOW.` · `THE THEATER FULL, THE SCHOOL EMPTY.` · `A STUDENT'S POSTURE, A LIVING MIND.` · then, large: `LEARN AS LONG AS I LIVE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've told yourself you're too old, too late or too settled to learn. A language, an instrument, a skill, a subject, a way of praying or thinking. Hold it lightly. Notice what the too-old voice sounds like, and whose voice it might be. Then picture yourself as Seneca in the third row: notebook open, unbothered by the smirks. What would the first small lesson be? The bell holds the time.
To school when old. Seneca sits in Metronax's lectures despite the mockery: learn as long as you don't know, which means as long as you live. Today's word.
Your line: learn as long as I live. Learn one new thing today, deliberately, from someone or something: a word, a fact, a skill. Take the first small lesson. Day four hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: People who take Seneca's advice keep learning at every age, often choosing one new subject or skill a year and approaching it as a beginner.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 76.3: one must keep learning as long as one doesn't know.

trapdoor: what you thought: school is for the young.
what it means: learning lasts as long as ignorance does, which is as long as you live.
what a scholar hears: Letters 76.1–4; Metronax is otherwise little known; the Naples theater detail (76.4) shows Greek culture alive in Neapolis.

notes: Letters 76.1: five days at Metronax's school; 76.3: 'tamdiu discendum est, quamdiu nescias; si proverbio credimus, quamdiu vivas'; 76.4: the packed theater at Naples. Confirm Latin and numbers.
The script says Seneca was 'sixty-something'; Letters 76 is usually dated to c. 64 CE, and Seneca's birth is usually put c. 4 BCE–1 CE, so he would be in his sixties. Confirm.
'Rich beyond counting' and 'former adviser to the emperor' are general biographical descriptions (Nero's adviser).
